The standard is endorsed by NHS England as required by the Health and Social Care Act 2012, and supported by NHS Blood and Transplant, the Royal College of Physicians and the UK Transfusion Laboratory Collaborative.
rows.implication: QS138 is what commissioners and audit teams actually measure against, so statement 2 is the lever that converts the NG24 change into procurement pressure. The admission that the national audit still measures the old "expected moderate blood loss" population means there is a measurement gap right now: trusts will be judged against a standard whose audit tool lags it. That is a legitimate, evidenced conversation opener with transfusion practitioners and theatre leads, and it dates the opportunity — the gap closes when the October 2026 QS138 audit runs.

maternity-neonatal.area: National Guidance, the Safety Reviews and the 2026 Reset

rows.ref: NICE NG235 — Intrapartum care
rows.kind: NICE guideline · published 29/09/2023 · replaces CG190 (2014)
rows.finding: NG235 covers care of women (and pregnant trans and non-binary people) and their babies during labour and immediately after birth, for term pregnancies (37–42 weeks). It updates and replaces the 2014 guideline CG190, helping women make informed choices about place of birth and labour care, and aims to reduce unwarranted variation in practice.
rows.implication: NG235 is the current authoritative benchmark for intrapartum care — any product, training or briefing aimed at NHS maternity services should reference it explicitly and by number.

rows.ref: NICE NG201 — Antenatal care
rows.kind: NICE guideline · published 19/08/2021 · updates CG62 (2008)
rows.finding: NG201 covers the routine antenatal care pregnant women and their babies should receive, including that a first (booking) appointment with a midwife should take place by 10+0 weeks of pregnancy. It updates and replaces the 2008 guideline CG62 and should be read alongside NG137, NG207, NG192 and NG235.
rows.implication: Still the current national standard for routine antenatal pathway design, so remains the correct reference point for any commissioning or training conversation about the antenatal pathway.

rows.ref: DHSC, The Renewed Women's Health Strategy for England (CP 1558, ISBN 978-1-5286-6262-8, 90 pages, published 15 April 2026); and Women's Health Strategy for England (CP 736, 2022) — withdrawn 20 May 2026
rows.kind: National policy — strategy replaced, both pages read live
rows.finding: The 2022 Women's Health Strategy for England now loads with "[Withdrawn]" in the page title and the line "This publication was withdrawn on 20 May 2026. The renewed Women's Health Strategy for England was published on 15 April 2026." The renewed strategy is a 90-page DHSC command paper, and GOV.UK's own description reads: "The renewed strategy is aligned with the 10 Year Health Plan for England and sets out how women will have voice, choice and power in their health and healthcare."
rows.implication: Every deck, bid and pathway document citing the 2022 Women's Health Strategy is quoting withdrawn policy, and has been since 20 May 2026. This is the highest-value single correction in the speciality because that strategy has been the standard opening slide for women's health business cases for four years. Two practical consequences: check any live bid before it goes out, and re-anchor the argument on the renewed strategy's alignment to the 10 Year Health Plan, which is where the money and the accountability now sit.

rows.ref: NHS England, Referral to Treatment Waiting Times statistical press notice, June 2026 (published 13/08/2026) — Table 1, RTT pathways by treatment function
rows.kind: Official statistics — figures read from the PDF and ranked by our own arithmetic
rows.finding: The Gynaecology Service treatment function held 575,870 incomplete RTT pathways at the end of June 2026, with 61.0% within 18 weeks against the NHS Constitution's 92% standard. Our own arithmetic on the same table puts that in context: gynaecology is the 4th largest waiting list of the 18 named clinical specialties (behind trauma and orthopaedics 829,590, ophthalmology 620,922 and ear nose and throat 594,546), the 5th worst on 18-week performance, and 8.1% of England's entire 7,147,562 incomplete pathways. Of gynaecology's completed pathways that month, 84.5% were non-admitted (92,071) against 15.5% admitted (16,892).
rows.implication: The 84.5% non-admitted split is the commercially important number, and it is the one nobody quotes. Gynaecology's bottleneck is overwhelmingly outpatient and diagnostic, not theatre — so a pitch built on operating-list throughput is aimed at 15.5% of the activity. The arguments that fit the actual constraint are one-stop and see-and-treat clinics, outpatient hysteroscopy, direct-access ultrasound and anything that resolves a woman in a single visit. Combined with the 61.0% performance and a 92% standard, gynaecology is a specialty under real, measurable, board-level pressure, which is the condition in which capacity propositions get heard.

ent-head-neck.area: Otology, Otitis Media and Ear Surgery

rows.ref: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Otitis media with effusion in under 12s. NICE guideline NG233, Rationale and impact section. Published 30 August 2023.
rows.kind: NICE guideline (committee rationale and health economic model)
rows.finding: NICE does not recommend grommet insertion for children whose glue ear has not caused hearing loss, stating there is no urgent need for surgery regardless of whether the effusion is persistent or transient. It describes the evidence that early grommets improve final hearing thresholds in the short term as very low quality. It recommends considering a single intraoperative application of ciprofloxacin drops (moderate-quality evidence of reduced otorrhoea at 6 weeks; low-quality for reduced tube blockage) but specifically does not recommend postoperative ciprofloxacin drops or injected ciprofloxacin, and advises keeping the ear dry for 2 weeks. The guideline’s own economic evaluation compared no intervention, hearing aids, grommets alone and grommets with adenoidectomy, and found grommets generally more cost effective than no intervention but with cost-effectiveness comparable to hearing aids and to grommets plus adenoidectomy.
rows.implication: If you sell ventilation tubes, hearing devices or otic drops, this is the document the commissioner will quote back. It kills any pitch built on hearing benefit in children without documented hearing loss, and it creates a defined, narrow, NICE-backed opening for a single intraoperative dose of ciprofloxacin drops while closing the far larger postoperative repeat-dosing market. The economic finding that grommets are no better value than hearing aids is the argument a hearing-device supplier should be making and a tube supplier should be ready for.

rows.ref: MacKeith S, Mulvaney CA, Galbraith K, Webster KE, Connolly R, Paing A, Marom T, Daniel M, Venekamp RP, Rovers MM, Schilder AG. Ventilation tubes (grommets) for otitis media with effusion (OME) in children. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2023, Issue 11, CD015215.pub2. Published 15 November 2023.
rows.kind: Cochrane systematic review of randomised controlled trials
rows.finding: 19 RCTs, 2,888 children. Compared with watchful waiting, early grommets made little to no difference to the proportion of children whose hearing had returned to normal after 8 to 10 years (93% with grommets versus 95% without; RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.03; 1 study, 391 participants; very low-certainty evidence), and little to no difference to persistent glue ear after 18 months to 6 years (15% versus 12%). Against no treatment, the odds ratio for return to normal hearing at 12 months was 1.13 (95% CI 0.46 to 2.74; 54% versus 51%), but grommets did reduce persistent effusion at six months (20.4% versus 68.0%; RR 0.30, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.65; low-certainty evidence). Persistent perforation was reported as 1.26% in one study of 635 ears.
rows.implication: Do not lead with long-term hearing outcomes in a children’s glue-ear conversation; a well-read ENT surgeon or commissioner will produce this review. The defensible claim is short-to-medium-term clearance of effusion, not durable hearing gain. It also explains why the market for long-acting or T-tubes is evidentially wide open - the review says explicitly that specific data on long-acting tubes is limited, which is an argument for a well-designed post-market study rather than a claim.

ophthalmology.area: The National Guidance Map and the Capacity Picture

rows.ref: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Glaucoma: diagnosis and management. NICE guideline NG81. Published 01/11/2017; last updated 26/01/2022; last reviewed 26/03/2025.
rows.kind: NICE guideline (NG)
rows.finding: NG81 makes 360-degree selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT), not eye drops, the first-line offer. Recommendation 1.4.4: "Offer 360° selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) to people with newly diagnosed OHT with IOP of 24 mmHg or more (excluding cases associated with pigment dispersion syndrome) if they are at risk of visual impairment within their lifetime"; recommendation 1.4.17 does the same for "newly diagnosed COAG that is not advanced". A generic prostaglandin analogue is the fallback under 1.4.6 and 1.4.19, offered only if the person declines SLT, SLT is unsuitable, they are waiting for SLT and need interim treatment, or SLT alone has not lowered IOP enough. Recommendations 1.4.5 and 1.4.18 both allow a second 360-degree SLT where the first has worn off. NG81 "updates and replaces NICE guideline CG85 (April 2009)". The 26/03/2025 entry added links to relevant technology appraisals and NICE states this "is not a change in practice".
rows.implication: Your glaucoma conversation is a capacity conversation, not an efficacy one. Every unit is expected to offer 360-degree SLT at diagnosis and most cannot deliver it at the volume NG81 implies — that is the gap to sell into, whether you carry lasers, consumables, clinic-throughput technology or a diagnostic pathway that identifies SLT candidates earlier. If you sell branded IOP-lowering drops, quote 1.4.19 back to yourself before the call: NICE names a generic PGA, so your case has to be built on the named exception routes, not on first-line displacement.

rows.ref: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Cataracts in adults: management. NICE guideline NG77. Published 26/10/2017; last reviewed 20/05/2025 (surveillance decision).
rows.kind: NICE guideline (NG)
rows.finding: Recommendation 1.2.2 is a single sentence and reps get tested on it: "Do not restrict access to cataract surgery on the basis of visual acuity." Recommendation 1.4.2 is equally blunt: "Do not offer multifocal intraocular lenses for people having cataract surgery." On biometry, 1.3.1 requires optical biometry for axial length, with ultrasound (1.3.2) only where optical is not possible or inaccurate; 1.3.5 specifies the intraocular lens (IOL) power formula by axial length — Haigis or Hoffer Q below 22.00 mm, Barrett Universal II between 22.00 and 26.00 mm "if it is installed on the biometry device and does not need the results to be transcribed by hand" and SRK/T if not, and Haigis or SRK/T above 26.00 mm. Critically, at the 20/05/2025 surveillance review NICE said it "reviewed this guideline and plan to update recommendations on intraocular lens selection" while explicitly declining to update biometry formulas, surgical timing and technique, bilateral simultaneous cataract surgery and toric lenses. Recommendations 1.4.1 and 1.4.4 currently read only: "the recommendations around lens design and material have been removed to allow for further consideration."
rows.implication: Two live commercial openings. First, 1.2.2 is the sentence to put in front of a commissioner running a visual-acuity referral threshold — that policy is non-compliant with NICE, and it is the argument that unlocks volume for anyone selling into a cataract pathway. Second, the IOL selection section is the one part of UK cataract guidance actively in play; if you sell premium, toric or extended-depth-of-focus lenses, your evidence dossier should be aimed at that update, and you must not let a field team read the blanked recommendations as a green light for multifocal.

colorectal-gi-endoscopy.area: National guidance, screening and the bowel cancer pathway

rows.ref: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). Suspected cancer: recognition and referral. NICE guideline NG12. Published 23/06/2015; last updated 15/04/2026.
rows.kind: NICE guideline
rows.finding: Section 1.3 sets the lower gastrointestinal referral pathway, and it is now FIT-led rather than symptom-led. Recommendation 1.3.1 [2023]: 'Offer quantitative faecal immunochemical testing (FIT) using HM-JACKarc or OC-Sensor to guide referral for suspected colorectal cancer in adults' — with an abdominal mass, a change in bowel habit, iron-deficiency anaemia, aged 40 and over with unexplained weight loss and abdominal pain, aged under 50 with rectal bleeding plus abdominal pain or weight loss, aged 50 and over with unexplained rectal bleeding, abdominal pain or weight loss, or aged 60 and over with anaemia even without iron deficiency. Recommendation 1.3.2 [2023]: 'Refer adults using a suspected cancer pathway referral for colorectal cancer if they have a FIT result of at least 10 micrograms of haemoglobin per gram of faeces.' Recommendation 1.3.5 keeps direct referral for a rectal mass without FIT.
rows.implication: This is the most useful single page in the NHS for anyone selling faecal immunochemical testing: NICE names only HM-JACKarc and OC-Sensor by brand. Any other FIT platform is selling into a pathway where NICE has not named it, so the buyer needs a local validation case rather than a guideline citation. For endoscopy suppliers, 10 µg Hb/g is the volume driver — it sets how many symptomatic patients reach a scope. Expect procurement conversations framed around FIT-negative safety netting (1.3.3) and sample-return rates (1.3.4), not test accuracy alone. Note also that NICE guideline NG151 covers management of diagnosed colorectal cancer, not referral; do not cite it for pathway questions.

rows.ref: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). Quantitative faecal immunochemical testing to guide colorectal cancer pathway referral in primary care. HealthTech guidance HTG690 (formerly Diagnostics guidance DG56). Published 24/08/2023; last reviewed 24/08/2023.
rows.kind: HealthTech guidance
rows.finding: This is the source document behind the FIT referral threshold, and its guidance number has changed. Recommendation 1.1 recommends quantitative FIT using HM-JACKarc or OC-Sensor to guide referral, and adds that 'FIT should be offered even if the person has previously had a negative FIT result through the NHS bowel cancer screening programme'. Recommendation 1.2 sets referral at 'a FIT result of at least 10 micrograms of haemoglobin per gram of faeces'. NICE states the guidance 'replaces NICE's diagnostics guidance on quantitative faecal immunochemical tests to guide referral for colorectal cancer in primary care (DG30)' and partially updates NG12. Recommendation 1.6 places six further tests — FOB Gold, IDK Hemoglobin ELISA, IDK Hemoglobin/Haptoglobin Complex ELISA, IDK TurbiFIT, NS-Prime and QuikRead go iFOBT — in a research-only category.
rows.implication: DG30 is dead and DG56 is a retired number. Anyone quoting either in a tender response, a clinical education pack or a value dossier is quoting a superseded reference, and an NHS procurement lead will notice. Cite HTG690. Commercially, the six tests parked in recommendation 1.6 are the live opening — NICE has not rejected them, it has said the accuracy estimates are too uncertain, which is an evidence-generation brief rather than a closed door. If you sell one of them, the route into an NHS pathway is a local accuracy study, not a guideline citation.
